#897. Aspyn Ovard Reveals 10-Year Secret Behind Parker Ferris Breakup

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County star Aspyn Ovard shared the decade-long secret that led to her divorce from Parker Ferris on the show’s premiere: "It was literally earth-shattering."

Aspyn Ovard is sharing her truth about the end of her marriage to Parker Ferris.

Two years after their divorce, the Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County star revealed the infamous “10-year secret” fans have long awaited to learn: the real reason behind her breakup from Ferris.

“Publicly, I'd never shared why we got divorced,” Ovard said on the Nov. 12 premiere of the first season of the Hulu series. “When Parker and I were getting married, we were definitely—I thought, actually—we were on the same page about where we stood with drinking and smoking and things like that.”

While the YouTuber—who shares daughters Cove, 7, Lola, 5, and Elle, 2, with her ex—assumed she and Ferris both abstained from alcohol, she learned her then-husband wasn’t being truthful.

“My dad struggled with alcoholism, so the only version of him that I knew was some level of intoxicated,” Ovard recalled. “Whenever he would come home, and just the sound of his work boots, just like a dark cloud, over the house.”

“Finding out that Parker had been drinking behind my back for years, it was literally earth-shattering,” she continued, nodding in agreement when a producer asked if that was the big secret. “He went through so much to hide it from me, and the fact that my husband, who was supposed to be the safest person, would do that to me.”

The 30-year-old became emotional as she shared how learning of Ferris' hidden behavior impacted her, while also revealing how the timing made the situation even more difficult.

As Ovard told the cameras, “For him to know what alcoholism did to my family, to find all of this out two months after my dad died from alcoholism hurt so bad.”

In April 2024, the influencer shocked fans when she filed for divorce from Ferris—whom she married in 2015 when she was just 19 years old—the same day she announced the birth of their third baby.

Following the divorce, Ovard hinted on social media that she uncovered a decade-long secret that led to the dissolution of her marriage, which led to years of speculation and theories from fans about what went wrong.

And now that the truth is out there once and for all, the mom of three believes fans may be a little disappointed.

“People are going to be underwhelmed with what it is,” Ovard told E! News in an interview during the Mormon Wives’ junket. “But I think seeing him talk about it and then seeing me cry about it, maybe will give some perspective.”

“I’m very curious to see what people will say,” she added, “because I’ve seen some crazy theories and it’s just not that crazy of a thing.”

While time will tell how fans will react, the reality described going through that difficult time as “overwhelming” for her. That said, she’s not sure if she would do anything differently.

“I don’t know if I would handle things the same way if I could go back two years ago and talk about that all again,” Ovard admitted. “There’s no way to really navigate life when you’re just doing it all for the first time.”

For a closer look at Ovard’s love life now amid her relationship with married couple Billy and Bri Davis, along with where her costars stand with their partners, keep reading…

Following her divorce from Cory Althoff, podcaster Bobbi Althoff is dating Tyler Hawkins, who plays a special role in Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County.

"He styles me, that’s how he supports me,” she told E! News in May, adding that the basketball player, "picks out my outfits every day. He styles me every day for the show. It’s great."

Aspyn Ovard, who filed for divorce from Parker Ferris in 2024 after eight years of marriage, is currently in a throuple relationship with married couple Billy Davis and Bri Davis.

After many ups and downs, Jen Affleck—who is pregnant with her and Zac Affleck's fourth baby—officially filed for divorce from her husband of seven years, E! News confirmed Nov. 4.

Despite ongoing relationship speculation, Salomé Andrea and Aaron Brimhall are still going strong as they prepare to welcome their third baby together. The duo, who married in 2012, also share 8-year-old twins Luca and Rue.

McCall DaPron—the sister of Mormon Wives' Mayci Neeley—shares four kids with husband Kirk DaPron, who she wed in 2011.

Ashleigh Pease and Nate Pease are rock solid after over a decade of marriage. "This 13th year together is one that has felt full circle!" she wrote on Instagram in September. "A season of fruits. Comfort. The happiest milestones."

Madison Bontempo and Kyler Steven Fisher, who wed in 2013, have been open about the highs and lows of their relationship. "Kyler and I aren’t perfect," she wrote on Instagram in October. "We’ve had arguments. We’ve had hard seasons. We’ve had moments we wish we could take back. And we’re not afraid to admit that."

But, she added, "Those moments aren’t our whole story. There’s also laughter, friendship, forgiveness, growth, five beautiful children, a million memories, and a love that has continued to evolve through every season of our lives."

Avery Woods and David Woods, parents to Ziggy and Stevie, are still feeling the love after a decade of marriage. As she simply put it, "my forever + always."

The future of flight meets space exploration as a futuristic electric aircraft hovers beside Blue Origin's massive New Glenn rocket stage.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A futuristic single-person aircraft takes to the skies at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, with the upper stage of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket providing a dramatic backdrop.

The unusual scene was captured during the MAX POWER event, which brought together innovators and emerging technologies at the iconic spaceflight facility.

The photograph shows a single-person electric aircraft called Jetson ONE, developed by Jetson, a US-based company working to bring personal flight to the skies.

The compact rotorcraft uses multiple propellers to climb into the air, allowing it to take off and vertically without the need for a runway.

The aircraft was performing flight demonstrations during the UP.Summit gathering, which formed part of the larger MAX POWER event at the Kennedy Space Center.

During the demonstrations, the Jetson ONE demonstrated its ability to maneuver through the air and hover in place, giving spectators a close-up look at the technology in action.

The photograph offers a fascinating glimpse at two very different approaches to flight. While Jetson is developing small electric aircraft designed for personal transportation, Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket is built to carry payloads far beyond Earth's atmosphere.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

#895. Is No 10 still the best, or No 41? The myths and maths of Premier League shirt numbers

While No 9s still score the most goals and No 1s try to stop them, trends have changed since the introduction of squad numbers in the early 1990s

How much is a shirt number worth? It costs £8 if you want two digits added to the back of Arsenal’s 2026-27 home shirt, whereas Manchester City add on £16 for customisation, whether you want a name as well as a number or not.

That is cheap compared to what baseball players decide among themselves. Juan Soto bought Brett Baty a $92,000 (£69,000) car in exchange for getting his preferred number (22) when he joined the New York Mets last year. But that’s baseball, where they allow players to wear ‘0’. Anything goes.

There’s a lot of choice in football, even if nobody has worn zero. According to Transfermarkt’s data, every number from one to 99 has been used at some point by at least one of the current Premier League clubs. Not until we go above 45 do we find a number that has been omitted by any of them. And it highlights how random these things can be once you reach the upper reaches of what is permitted, as Brentford and Manchester City have never had a No 46 but have issued a No 99 and No 98 respectively.

The weirdest anomaly is Chelsea not having had a player wear higher than No 81 when it seemed like they were making that many signings every summer. Or maybe the strangest state of affairs is at Everton, who are on to their second No 10 of the 2026-27 season when they haven’t got a No 7 or a No 9. Riddle me that, Toffees.

Fixed squad numbers are a relatively recent development within the history of football. Numbered shirts were first introduced in 1911, with the starting players normally wearing No 1 to No 11 until the 1990s. Iconic footballers have always gravitated towards the key numbers; Kenny Dalglish wore No 7 for Liverpool, bestowing immense value upon that shirt. But if he was unavailable, then someone else would wear it. These days, numbers may be more important to a given player than the club they represent. They become part of their brand.

Opta have data on Premier League goals scored by different shirts since 1993, when the competition introduced squad numbers. The top five are between seven and 11. Traditional numbers still carry the most weight. The standings thereafter are less obvious. Thierry Henry did some heavy lifting for No 14 but there have still been almost 1,300 goals from others who have worn the number. Thinking of players who contributed even a decent chunk towards the 1,100-plus goal tallies for the shirts between 17 and 20 is not easy.

Far more than goals determine player worth. Transfermarkt use the wisdom of crowds to establish a theoretical market value for every player based on numerous factors. It’s a guide, rather than definitively what a footballer would cost to buy from their current club.

With this data we can see which shirt numbers are the most valuable in the 2026-27 Premier League. There is no real pattern on an individual level. The 13 footballers who are believed to be worth at least €100m share 10 different numbers between them, with No 11 the most notable omission from the group. This wouldn’t have happened during Mohamed Salah’s peak.

There is also only one No 9 in the top eight, though Erling Haaland is the most valuable player in the Premier League. Despite João Pedro also being in the €100m club, the highest cumulative total market value (€766m) across the division belongs to No 10, ahead of No 9 (€752m) and No 7 (€683.5m). None of these shirts has the highest average, though. When it comes to valuing a number, take quality over quantity.

If you don’t support Chelsea, Manchester United or Newcastle, you probably can’t name the player who wears their number No 41 shirt. You might struggle even if you are a fan. But with Arsenal’s Declan Rice on hand to accompany Estêvão, Harry Amass and Jacob Ramsey respectively, No 41 has the highest average market value in the Premier League.

These standings would have been different in seasons past, with likely more than four of the traditional 1-11 in the top 10. At various points in 2018 or 2019, N’Golo Kanté and Raheem Sterling were estimated to be worth at least €100m while wearing No 7 shirts, with Eden Hazard, Harry Kane and Sadio Mané of similarly high value when sporting No 10. But No 41 is the shirt number that is worth the most on average today, thanks largely to Rice.

#894. Ghana kick-start Afcon 2027 bid despite Ayew penalty miss

Jordan Ayew joined Championship side Sheffield United in September after spending two seasons with Leicester City

Ghana belatedly kick-started their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) qualifying campaign with a 2-0 home win over Somalia.

The Black Stars had lost their opening two Group C matches against Ivory Coast and The Gambia, leading to the departure of coach Carlos Queiroz by mutual consent.

Ghana women's coach Kim Bjorkegren was placed in interim charge for this month's double-header against the Ocean Stars, with the West Africans in danger of missing a second successive edition of the Afcon finals.

The hosts were given a chance to take an early lead in Sekondi-Takoradi after Alidu Seidu was pulled down in the box, but Jordan Ayew's 14th-minute penalty was saved by Somalia goalkeeper Ibrahim Hussein.

Ghana did go ahead in first-half stoppage time when Mohammed Salisu headed Mohammed Kudus's deep corner back across goal and Jonas Adjetey nodded in from six yards out.

Felix Afena-Gyan doubled the Black Stars' advantage just after the hour mark when his shot from inside the box squirmed under Hussein and over the line.

The four-time continental champions remain six points behind group leaders Ivory Coast, who extended their 100% record by beating The Gambia 2-1 in Bouake.

Brighton midfielder Malick Yalcouye tucked in from seven yards out and Elye Wahi slotted home to double the Elephants' lead before Musa Barrow pulled one back for the visitors before the break.

Elsewhere on Thursday, there were wins for Cameroon, DR Congo and Senegal, who all remain on track to qualify for next year's tournament in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.

The third round of qualifying fixtures continues on Friday with Egypt, Morocco, Nigeria and South Africa in action among 12 fixtures.

Nicolas Jackson has 11 goals in 17 appearances for club and country this season

Nicolas Jackson set Senegal on their way to a 4-1 home win over Sudan in Group J, with Aston Villa team-mate Ibrahim Mbaye also on the scoresheet for Patrick Vieira's men in Dakar.

The Teranga Lions lead the standings on seven points, three ahead of Mozambique, who host Ethiopia on Friday.

Cameroon also remained unbeaten and moved on to seven points in Group G with a comfortable 2-0 victory over Namibia in Douala.

Meanwhile, Newcastle United striker Yoane Wissa opened the scoring as DR Congo continued their perfect start with a 3-1 triumph over Sierra Leone in Kinshasa.

The Leopards are on nine points at the top of Group E, five points ahead of Zimbabwe and Equatorial Guinea after those two sides drew 0-0.

Nigeria were handed a boost after Group L leaders Guinea-Bissau could only manage a 1-1 draw in their away tie against Madagascar in neutral Morocco.

The Super Eagles trail Guinea-Bissau by four points ahead of their home game against Tanzania on Friday (16:00 GMT).

Tanzania are assured of a place at Afcon 2027 as tournament co-hosts, with the other three sides battling for one qualification spot.

And Benin bolstered their bid to reach back-to-back finals with a 4-1 win over Central African Republic.

Gernot Rohr's Cheetahs lead Group F by three points from Burkina Faso, who entertain Mauritania on Friday.

In Group D, another section with just one spot available, Guinea moved level on points with table-toppers South Africa after seeing off Eritrea 2-1 in Conakry.

"We just don't have enough people, and we're looking for more," one NASA astronaut told Space.com.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If NASA ever hopes to build a permanent moon base for astronauts, let alone aim for Mars, the U.S. space agency is going to need a whole lot of space travelers. And now, you have a chance to be one of them.

NASA on Saturday (Nov. 7) put out the call for a new class of astronaut candidates who think they have the "right stuff" to fly, live and work in space. Those astronaut hopefuls have until Dec. 3 to apply (the application website is here), with NASA planning to make its final selections in late 2027.

"This is an extraordinary time to join NASA's astronaut corps," the space agency's chief, Jared Isaacman, said in an announcement, which was made during NASA's "Max Power" air show at Kennedy Space Center (KSC) in Florida. "The people we select could walk on the moon, live and work at the Moon Base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars."

It's been two years since NASA last sought applications for astronauts. In 2024, more than 8,000 people applied, though only 10 — five men and five women — made the cut. They're in the middle of a two-year training program right now.

This new 2027 astronaut group will be the 25th astronaut class in NASA history. Its announcement comes the same year that NASA returned astronauts to the moon for the first time since the Apollo era with the Artemis II moon flyby. Four more astronauts will test Artemis moon landers in Earth orbit on the Artemis III mission in 2027.

NASA currently has 32 active astronauts in its spaceflying corps. The agency has recruited 370 people to fly in space since 1959, when the first seven Mercury astronauts were selected and unveiled to the world.

"There is a lot to be done in order to get all of these new vehicles and the new suits and everything as we continue to work towards the moon, build a base there, stay permanently, and then eventually onto Mars," NASA astronaut Nichole Stilwell, class of 2021, told Space.com in an interview at KSC during the Max Power event. "And so we just don't have enough people, and we're looking for more."

If you're interested in applying to be a NASA astronaut, you should take a look at the requirements first.

NASA's core guidelines require applicants to be U.S. citizens and have a master's degree in a STEM field like "engineering, biological science, physical science, or computer science from an accredited institution," the space agency said in a statement. You'll also need at least three years of experience in your related field.

Don't have a master's degree? Here's three other ways NASA might consider your application, according to the agency's advisory:

If you're a medical doctor and are considering applying to be an astronaut, your residency training can be counted toward your professional experience, but only if it is completed by July 2027, NASA said.

If you want to be a pilot astronaut for NASA, you'll need some serious flight hours under your belt. Here's a rundown of some ways to meet that requirement:

"For those who apply, becoming a NASA astronaut is more than a career opportunity,” said NASA chief astronaut Scott Tingle, who also chairs the Astronaut Selection Board at the agency's Johnson Space Center (JSC) in Houston. "It is a chance to join a legacy of explorers who have pushed the boundaries of discovery and play a role in the missions that will shape humanity’s future in space."

Once NASA selects its 2027 astronaut class, the new recruits can expect to begin a two-year training program based out of JSC, which is home to the agency's astronaut corp and Mission Control.

“The window is open. The mission is waiting.," NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson said in a statement. "And the only thing missing from the greatest adventure humanity has ever embarked upon is you."

Space.com Content Manager Chelsea Gohd contributed to this report from NASA's Max Power event at the Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida.

#892. Beyoncé Reveals New Details of “Very Small” Wedding to Jay-Z

Nearly 20 years after Beyoncé and Jay-Z tied the knot in a surprise 2008 ceremony, the “Crazy in Love” singer revealed ultra-rare details of their wedding.

After Jay-Z put a ring on it, Beyoncé had one must-have for their wedding.

The “Crazy in Love” singer recently shared ultra-rare insight into her and the “Empire State of Mind” rapper’s 2008 nuptials—including how her mother Tina Knowles ensured she loved the day like XO.

“My favorite dress my mother designed was my wedding dress,” the 45-year-old—mom to Blue Ivy, 14, as well as 9-year-old twins Rumi and Sir with Jay-Z—told i-D in an interview published Nov. 11. “It was gorgeously simple and made with her love.”

And the dress was the cherry, or love, on top of an otherwise perfect day.

“We have a very small wedding in our home,” she continued. “We told guests we were having a party, and no one knew they were coming to our wedding but our parents and a few friends.”

For Beyoncé, wearing a dress designed by her mother was a “very important” detail of her big day, adding, “more important than any designer dress.”

The “Break My Soul” singer and Jay-Z (real name Shawn Carter) are clearly feeling nostalgic for the journey they’ve taken both in love and their career.

After all, Jay-Z recently debuted his docuseries Jay-Z in 8 on HBO Max in September, which examines his life and career in eight episodes.

“I’m really excited,” Jay-Z told E! News of his family sharing in the milestone. “They know these things. We talk all the time. It'll be fascinating to see on a big screen and at times, I know it'll be, like, cringe.”

Although the rapper runs this town, he admitted he wasn’t feeling as bold when it came to getting vulnerable in front of his little ones.

“You know, when you put yourself out there like that,” he added, “you get embarrassed.”

Nevertheless, he emphasized, “It’s honest, and it's a beautiful piece. I'm very proud of it.”

And having both his career retrospective—his debut album Reasonable Doubt just celebrated its 30th anniversary in June—and milestone coincide felt especially kismet.

“It's just all aligned,” he said. “We didn't plan on it being part of a 30-year celebration. We were just, you know, creating a piece that we both believed in, and it just so happened it all lined up.”

For a deeper look into Beyoncé and Jay-Z’s love story, keep reading…

#891. Which football club has had most international captains in the same team? | The Knowledge

Plus: more speedy marathons by footballers, headed goals of the season and chairs acting as managers

Mail us with all of your questions and answers

“Which club team has had the most international captains playing together at one time?” asks MH Zahid. “Conversely, which international team has had the most club captains in its starting lineup at one time?”

A quick web search finds a fuss being made in various corners of the internet of Chelsea’s 2009-10 squad because it contained six national team captains in Michael Ballack (Germany), Petr Cech (Czech Republic), Didier Drogba (Côte d’Ivoire), Branislav Ivanovic (Serbia), Mikel John Obi (Nigeria) and John Terry (England). These are, indeed, six people who captained their countries, playing together at one time, but crucially they were not all international captains at that time, which because we like to have our hands bound as tight as possible – no questions please – mean they are disqualified from this particular tournament. Ivanovic, you see, was not named Serbia captain until 2012 and Mikel, who was but a whippersnapper at 22 when the 2009-10 season started, was still seven years from getting his hands on the Nigeria armband.

But if that Chelsea team are not themselves the best answer that Knowledge has come up with, they are at least associated with them, having been knocked out of the Champions League by José Mourinho’s captain-strewn Inter. Inter ended up beating Bayern Munich 2-0 in the final, with a team that included the then full-time captains of Brazil (Lúcio), Romania (Cristian Chivu), Cameroon (Samuel Eto’o) and Macedonia (Goran Pandev), while the captain of Serbia (Dejan Stankovic) came off the bench to replace Chivu in the second half and Pandev was replaced by Sulley Muntari, who while not Ghana’s full-time captain had led the side in their most recent game, a 2-1 defeat at Bosnia and Herzegovina that March.

But that’s not all! Among the unused substitutes was Iván Córdoba, who at this point in his career had lost Colombia’s armband to Mario Yepes but been given it back for their previous game, against Paraguay, in the absence of his fellow centre-back. Also in the team and worthy of note, if not of inclusion in our tally of then captains, were Wesley Sneijder, occasional Netherlands skipper and still their all-time record appearance maker, and Javier Zanetti, who regularly captained Argentina and is No 4 on their list of all-time appearance makers (he would be higher had he not been frozen out by their then manager, Diego Maradona, before the 2010 World Cup), with occasional Kenya captain McDonald Mariga also among the subs.

By our count that’s seven players in one matchday squad who could boast of being their country’s current captain at kick-off, and none of whom captained their club side – that honour went to Zanetti. Our searches have not found another team to match that one, but readers have suggested a couple who came close, in the shape of Tottenham in 2020-21 (who boasted five international captains at the time in Hugo Lloris of France; Serge Aurier of Côte d’Ivoire; South Korea’s Son Heung-min; Gareth Bale of Wales; and England’s own Harry Kane, suggested by John Curry) and Liverpool just last year, when in Conor Bradley, Andy Robertson, Virgil van Dijk, Wataru Endo, Mo Salah and Dominik Szoboszlai they had six – though they never played together while they were all incumbent international captains. Any more for any more?

The fastest former footballer we found in time for last week’s instalment was Alexei Smertin, the former Russia and Chelsea midfielder, who screamed around the Kazan Marathon course in 2020 in just two hours, 48 minutes and 17 seconds. But as Richard Askham emailed to point out, that has since been bettered by Joe Skarz, formerly of Bury, Rotherham and Oxford United, and current manager of Golcar United of the Northern Counties East League Premier Division, who in 2025 finished the Yorkshire Marathon with a chip time of 2hr 47min 33sec.

The next question is what level of football do you need to reach to qualify as a footballer? Because Stig Lindmark tipped us off about the former AIK academy player Andreas Almgren, whose dreams of football glory were derailed by injury in his teens and eventually shifted his focus towards distance running. In New York at the start of this month – while the retired cyclist Tom Dumoulin was putting most former footballers to shame with a time of 2:27:12 – he ran his first ever marathon and only went and won the thing, in 2hr 6min 1sec. With no senior competitive appearances he probably does not count, but it’s a good enough effort to get a mention.

“Has a headed goal ever been awarded goal of the season,” wonders Rupert Sheard. “I can think of a few belters, but awards tend to go to ones kicked in.”

“The closest I could get was Robin van Persie’s flying header at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, for the Netherlands against Spain,” writes Sinan Eccles. “He was pipped to the official goal of the tournament by James Rodríguez’s iconic volley, but did make it to third in that year’s Puskas Award – behind Rodríguez and Stephanie Roche.”

Peter Tomlin writes: “Having researched the goal of the season awards in many countries, the only header I could find that won was Keith Houchen’s fantastic one in the 1986-87 FA Cup Final for Coventry v Tottenham. However, Alisson’s dramatic 95th-minute headed winner v West Brom was voted Liverpool’s goal of the season for the 2020-21 season.”

And Mark Johnson points out that Basile Boli’s ridiculous bullet header for Marseille against PSG at the end of the 1993 season would surely have won the Ligue 1 goal of the season award but for the inconvenient fact that no such award existed at the time.

Martyn Amos has responded to last week’s scepticism about the possibility of an Ipswich fan website existing in 1990, the year before the first known website went online. “Just to clarify, the original page was set up by Phil Clarke, who was working at BT Labs in Martlesham (near Ipswich), in 1990,” he writes. “At the time, as I said, the web was still experimental, and I think the page was only available internally. Your correspondent is correct in saying that the first public website appeared in August 1991. But the ITFC page still existed, in some recognisable form, using the standard web technology, in 1990, so I think it counts. That’s my understanding, anyway.”

With Lee Power taking charge of Swindon Town, in last week’s Knowledge archive we dug up our piece from 2006 on chairs acting as managers, we wrote in October 2015. Neil Bellis, the director of communications at Chester FC, writes to point out we missed Terry Smith off our list.

“He took over four games into the season despite not really knowing much about ‘soccer’,” writes Neil. “He was a former American Football coach but for some reason ending up buying our club. Not only did we end up getting relegated from the Football League for the first time in 1999-2000 we also saw a few very strange ideas from him including having a team talk as the Lord’s prayer and appointing a captain in defence, midfield and attack. Thankfully we are now fan owned so this level of insanity shouldn’t happen again.”

One of Smith’s first games as manager was against Aston Villa in the League Cup, a fixture that prompted a visit from ITV to see what was going on. The result of that visit can be seen here:

“There’s nothing magical about being a coach,’ said Smith not long after his arrival. “It’s like being the general manager of a business, the coaching principles are the same in any sport.” That doesn’t sound too promising but things didn’t really go horribly wrong until the end of November, when Chester began a run of 11 defeats in 12 matches. There’s some footage here of the aftermath of the 5-1 home defeat by Leyton Orient just after Christmas – “I want to thank you guys,” says Smith in the dressing room. “That’s the most pitiful, pitiful effort I’ve ever damn seen.”

Smith stepped down as manager and brought in Ian Atkins in January 2000, then sold the club in October 2001.

“What’s the highest score by a team or in a match where no player scored more than one goal?” writes Paul Gage.

“Manchester United have 20 league titles, won by three managers. Liverpool have 20 league titles won by 10. Which teams have the most and fewest titles won by the most and fewest managers?” asks Will Marquand.

“Djed Spence (shirt No 99) set up Pio Esposito (No 94) in Inter’s 2-0 win over Como at the weekend. Has there ever been a combination for a goal (assist and scorer) with a higher combined shirt number than 193?” writes Joe Strawson.

“Did the Fenerbahce side have more combined Premier League appearances than Liverpool in the teams’ recent Champions League match? If so was this the first instance of a club in Europe playing opposition who had more game appearances in their own league than they had themselves?” ponders Josh Wolff-Martin.

#890. Young duo at heart of Nations League's meanest defence

Northern Ireland play Ukraine in Belfast on Saturday before travelling to Budapest to face Hungary on Tuesday

Across his two spells as Northern Ireland boss, Michael O'Neill has been blessed with no shortage of centre-back talent.

Jonny Evans, Aaron Hughes, Gareth McAuley and Craig Cathcart were mainstays of his first stint in charge - so much so that, in some of the biggest games of O'Neill's managerial career at Euro 2016, the quartet all started across a flat back-four.

Since returning to the job four years ago, O'Neill has switched to three at the back, with Sunderland duo Trai Hume and Dan Ballard providing an injection of Premier League quality in what remains a side largely drawn from the Championship and League One.

But with Hume, something of a Swiss army knife in the squad, covering the injured Conor Bradley on the right flank and even starting in centre midfield against Ukraine last month, and Ballard presently nursing an injured hamstring, change has been required through this Nations League campaign.

Despite those forced alterations in defence, the side go into their concluding Group B2 fixtures against Ukraine and Hungary top of their pool and the only side at any level of the competition yet to concede a goal.

At the heart of their defensive efforts have been Ruairi McConville and Tom Atcheson, two young centre-backs already described by their international manager as having "no ceiling".

Birthdays and broken lamps - at home with the Charles brothers

NI can draw on strong club form in key window

At 21-years-old, Norwich City's McConville is the more senior of the pair.

Having been given his debut off the bench at home to Belarus two years ago this week, among the former Brighton man's early international assignments was trying to keep a rampant Alexander Isak in check during a 5-1 defeat by Sweden.

In the short time since he has looked an increasingly commanding figure, leading this Nations League group in clearances made with both head and boot.

"It would be unbelievable to keep that record for these last two games and go the whole of the campaign," he said of what is Northern Ireland's longest run without conceding a goal since 2017.

McConville notes that the streak is a team effort and product of collective work-rate, rather than just the defensive three alone.

"We're a team that works hard, a team that doesn't want to give anything up.

"We're confident in ourselves and we know that we're a good side."

It is McConville who has taken on the Ballard role in the middle of the defence for the past three games, with Atcheson on the right and Oxford United's Ciaron Brown, himself superb through the campaign so far, playing from the left.

On the developing understanding between an emerging unit, McConville added: "We're enjoying playing together.

"It's still early days together and we have to keep taking it game by game and doing what the gaffer tells us and the work on the training pitch.

"We don't have much time together when we're here [in international camp] so it's important to do all we can."

Watch on BBC iPlayer and BBC Two NI from19:15 GMT; Listen on BBC Sounds and BBC Radio Ulster; Watch, listen, live text and clips on BBC Sport app & website

Atcheson's comfort on the ball has been an asset across his six caps

After 16 caps, McConville is a relative veteran compared to Atcheson, who made his international bow in a friendly against Wales in March at a time when he had only four senior club starts to his name at Blackburn Rovers.

The most recent of those had come under O'Neill, then in a short stint as caretaker manager at the Championship club.

Clearly impressed by what he saw from the now 20-year-old at Ewood Park, Atcheson made his first Northern Ireland start against Guinea in June, a game in which he scored the winner with a fabulous flick before later being shown a red card.

Some 428 minutes into his international career, Atcheson is still to experience what it feels like to concede a goal.

The England-born defender feels Ballard "is definitely a big miss" to the side, but believes the squad's understanding of O'Neill's desired system is an asset to those who have starred during the Sunderland man's latest absence.

"I feel like everyone knows what they need to do, everyone knows their job, the details of the formation we play and system," he said.

"That's so key and I think that's why we're so solid defensively.

"It's a team thing, we're set up right, we're very on it all the time and everyone gives their all."

The first trailer for Other World: A Stranger Things Adventure doesn't show much, but there are enough clues for fans to figure out what it's about here.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

So, you thought "Stranger Things" was done and dusted after all that Conformity Gate nonsense? No way! Netflix's sci-fi sensation returns in the live-action prequel series "Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure."

Created by the Duffer Brothers and Kate Trefry, with the episodes set to be directed by Joe Wright ("Darkest Hour", "Black Mirror"), this new show isn't set in Hawkins or the electric '80s. No, this time around, the action takes place in Marion, Nevada, in 1955, and you know what else is located in Nevada, right? Area 51.

The teaser trailer certainly teases the possibility of a trip to the world's most paradoxically famous secret military base, showcasing a bike and radio resting outside of a fence with a sign that clearly says it's a restricted area (in any TV show or film, that's actually an invitation to see what's on the other side). Of course, the tease doesn't end there, as the thunder booms in the sky and there's a visual hint of a wormhole.

No story details about "Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure" have been released to date, but there are some clues out there for all the Internet sleuths.

Trefrey wrote the Henry Creel-focused "Stranger Things: The First Shadow" play, while Matt Duffer explained to Variety how a spin-off show would tackle the rock that Henry found in the briefcase in "Stranger Things." So, yes, expect this to be a Henry-centric affair and the start of his long, hard road to hell and becoming Vecna.

What'll be interesting, though, is to see how the show ties into the history of Area 51. After all, it was on April 12, 1955, that CIA officer Richard Bissell discovered the site, while the "Other Worlds" trailer has the date of April 19th clearly marked onscreen, so the timelines align nicely here.

"Stranger Things" has never been shy of tying itself to real-world science and historical events, so it'll be fascinating to see how the show explores Area 51 as a concept and the secrets everybody believes are hidden there.

Was it really a site to test highly advanced weapons and aircraft, or was E.T.'s cousin held hostage there until he revealed Colonel Sanders' 11 herbs and spices? Who knows, with all this renewed excitement around this mysterious military facility, we might get another "Storm Area 51" event to enjoy and laugh at all over again.

Regardless, more "Stranger Things" is welcome news, and since it's presumably about one of the show's best characters, Henry Creel, it only adds another layer to his already intriguing lore. If we can't have an origin story about Hopper's incredible and envious moustache, this is the next best thing.

"Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure" arrives on Netflix in 2028.

#888. Efficient catalyst-controlled C–H arylation of arenes

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Direct arylation of C–H bonds in arenes offers a streamlined alternative to widely used cross-coupling reactions.1 However, native substrates lack the preinstalled functional handles that ordinarily provide both reactivity and control over the site of reaction. Consequently, despite long-standing interest in directly engaging C–H bonds as reactive sites,2–4 the design of general catalysts that deliver high yields across diverse substrate classes while controlling site selectivity remains a challenge.5–12 Here we show that a microenvironment around a prototypical palladium dicarboxylate catalytic site can provide high selectivity for direct arylation of sterically exposed C–H sites, while high efficiency is achieved using an advanced palladium(II) precatalyst and tailored diaryliodonium reagents for selective aryl transfer. The applicability of this system spans from electron-rich to electron-deficient arenes, while electron-neutral benzene, which is often a challenge for C–H arylation, undergoes successive sterically controlled arylations, delivering functionalized polyaryl compounds. In addition to removing the necessity for pre-functionalized substrates, the mild conditions enable direct late-stage C–H arylation and the installation of aryl groups equipped with functionalities that are typically either reactive in traditional cross-coupling catalysis, such as triflates, iodides, and boronate esters, or sensitive to the basic conditions, such as N-hydroxysuccinimide esters. The results emphasize the distinct synthetic value of palladium-catalyzed direct C–H arylation reactions and showcase a catalyst platform that facilitates high yields and control over site-selectivity.

#887. Survivor’s Brady Booker Reveals Shocking Fate of Severed Thumb

Survivor 51’s Brady Booker shared the bizarre fate of his injured thumb after he sliced off a "quarter” of the finger, which led to his surprising exit from the jury on the Nov. 11 episode.

Brady Booker may have lost much of his thumb on Survivor, but he left with a new accessory.

After the professional wrestler was eliminated from the competition series, he shocked viewers during the Nov. 11 episode by exiting the jury so he could receive medical attention for his severed finger. But now he’s sharing how the chopped off “quarter” of his thumb was able to make it home to the U.S. from Fiji—and revealing its unusual fate.

“It was sitting in a cooler,” Booker told Parade in a Nov. 11 interview, recalling what happened to his partial thumb in the days after he was voted off season 51 on Day 14. “And then when time arose, when people started asking questions about it, they asked me what I wanted to do with it.”

“There was kind of a talk that you can’t bring flesh across international waters; I guess I never really thought of that,” he continued. “As white as it was at the time, it kind of looked like a scallop still in the shell, so maybe we could pass as that.”

But instead of the 27-year-old’s severed thumb being reattached to his hand, it was turned into jewelry.

“They ended up putting it in some resin, putting it in a necklace,” Booker revealed. “When I got back, we put a clasp on it.”

The shocking reveal came after host Jeff Probst shared Booker decided he wasn’t going to be able to outwit, outplay and outlast on the island as a member of the jury, becoming the first player to leave the jury in show’s history.

“First, a little business,” Probst explained to the players on the Nov. 11 episode. “Last night, immediately following Tribal Council, Brady asked to go home to tend to his injured thumb. So, Brady is out of the game. He’s gone, and will not be a member of the jury.”

While Booker’s historic decision to leave Fiji was on Day 14 of the competition, his now-infamous injury occurred 10 days prior.

It was on the fourth day of the competition—which was chronicled on the Sept. 30 episode—when Booker accidentally cut off a “quarter” of his thumb while chopping firewood with a machete.

After acknowledging this “stupid” mistake, he detailed what went down while being looked at in the medical tent.

“I was just splitting some wood to get to the dry center with the axe," Booker explained to the doctor. “Had a little corner of my thumb, that little corner right there, and I just lopped it off. I truly feel like I can still compete and hopefully, we can do something.”

His wish was granted, with Booker expressing his relief that he was given the all-clear to continue after his thumb was wrapped.

“When Doc told me I can still be in this game, it was like a new life," he reflected. "Sure, it's still a little numb, but I can touch all the fingers. I can touch the far end. I can clap. I can grab. Sure, Brody, pain exists. But I'd rather feel pain than nothing at all.”

And while he was ultimately sent home—with a new necklace—he’s far from the only castaway to face a rocky journey on the island. Keep reading for a closer look at all of the players on Survivor 51…

#886. SFA in talks with Boston officials over biennial friendly match

The Tartan Army made a big impression on the city of Boston during the World Cup

BBC Scotland has learned that the SFA is in active discussions aimed at a biennial friendly match being held in Boston.

Scotland played two World Cup matches in the US city during the summer and now the governing body and the state of Massachusetts are in talks aimed at building the bonds made between locals and the Tartan Army, through football.

More discussions are due to take place between the SFA and a delegation of state senators ahead of Scotland's Nations League match against North Macedonia at Hampden on Friday.

It has not yet been decided who will play in the game but BBC Scotland understands it will involve the Scoland national team.

US state senator Paul Feeney has been in the UK this week for talks around energy, but wanted to visit Scotland to build on the bonds made between the Tartan Army and those who partied with them for two weeks in June.

The state of Massachusetts has also passed a bill aimed at strengthening ties with Scotland after an estimated 25,000 fans partied in Boston and surrounding areas.

"We felt that this summer was more than just a football match, more than just, you know, 90 minutes at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough," Feeney said.

"It was a couple of weeks of these relationships being held, and you don't see that often. And I'm glad we got to experience it. And, frankly, we don't want that to end."

He added: "One of the things that we've been active on in Massachusetts today is to kind of take the lessons that we've learned, put together the best practices, and say, ok, we understand that we can't have a World Cup every year, but where we have such a strong connection with people in Scotland, could we do some sort of invitational tournament?

"To have that cultural exchange to kind of prop up economic development, and more than that, just to come together, have a few drinks, and enjoy each other's company."

Scotland fans placed cones on several Boston statues during their time in the city

Feeney said the Massachusetts Senate voted unanimously to support the concept.

"We're trying to work that through the legislature, get it to the finish," he said.

Talks aimed at organising a regular fixture are at an early stage but the SFA is already in advanced negotiations with businesses in Massachusetts about investment in the Scottish game.

"The Tartan Army invaded Massachusetts and I have to say they lit a spark that set off fireworks," Massachusetts Senate president Karen Spilka told BBC Scotland.

"They were sorely missed by so many people when they left.

"I think that by making the effort to come here and meet people and talk about tourism and economic development, we can start talking about things like Tartan Day and maybe having other events going on."

#885. ‘Second ball’ may be a Sunday league mantra but Yates showed its top-flight relevance

Midfielder’s old-school attributes came to the fore during Nottingham Forest’s win against Manchester City

Modern football is more systematised and data-driven than ever but some things never change. Winning the first ball is important but the second ball – the holy grail for Sunday league footballers – is often more so.

Nottingham Forest’s 3-1 win against Manchester City last weekend featured a classic example. Forest led 2-1 inside the last 20 minutes but City, lifted by Rayan Cherki’s sweet half-volley, were pushing for an equaliser.

Another City attack comes down their right: after Jair Cunha’s clearing header from a deep Matheus Nunes cross, the ball loops up in the air before descending inside the home penalty area.

Ryan Yates, Forest’s old-fashioned midfield general, is being pressed from behind by the Argentina international Enzo Fernández as the ball drops. Yates stands his ground, using his strength to hold off his opponent’s muscular challenge. Fernández tries to impose himself, too, but ends up on the turf.

Not only does Yates win that crucial one-on-one, by cleverly improvising an overhead kick to shift the ball away from danger he inadvertently begins a counterattack that arguably changes the course of Forest’s season.

Liam Delap shepherds the ball to Morgan Gibbs-White. Enzo Maresca’s team are hopelessly exposed and Gibbs-White devours the space in front of him with a driving run.

He lays a pass off to Delap, who takes one touch before swerving a sensational shot into the far corner for 3-1. It is a memorable move that will surely compete for goal of the month. But none of it would have been possible without the dirty work of Yates: a show of strength and desire from the captain at the other end of the pitch.

Oliver Glasner understands the importance of the moment and sprints to celebrate with his players. After a barren scoring run Delap suddenly has two goals in one afternoon. The home fans are delirious. Twelve seconds after Yates won the duel, Forest have a two-goal cushion rather than a desperate fight to maintain their lead.

The second ball is a pleasingly old-school term but remains of paramount importance. Visit your local amateur club and you are likely to hear it being shouted as a motivational mantra.

At grassroots level it’s a reminder to teammates that finesse and creativity are all very well, but it’s hard work, desire and a refusal to let your opponent get the better of you that win matches.

And it remains part of the elite game’s lexicon. Premier League managers sometimes point to upcoming opponents’ second-ball prowess – a back-handed compliment if ever there was one. The hidden meaning: “They feed off scraps at set pieces. They don’t create from open play.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

After seeing Southampton Under-21s lose to Wealdstone in the National League Cup a couple of years ago, I mentioned to the then Saints manager, Simon Rusk, that his goalkeeper had been shouting “second ball” throughout.

“To be honest,” Rusk replied with amusing frankness, “I’m not sure some of them even know what second ball means.”

Managers like relying on data. They like predictable outcomes. They prefer to remove risk, reduce chaos and exert control over as much of the game as possible. But while the outcome of a one-on-one duel can never be certain, the consequences can often be far-reaching. That’s why second balls matter.

Against City Yates was named in Forest’s starting lineup, and given the captain’s armband, for the first time this season. Glasner, asked how he had motivated his players, revealed: “Ryan Yates spoke. I played more than 500 games as a player, I’ve managed, I don’t know, 500 games … and I’ve never heard such an inspiring speech.”

Glasner’s captain backed up stirring words with action. If there was a sense Yates’s star was fading – that his attributes of graft, tenacity and box-to-box drive were losing currency – then it was emphatically extinguished at the City Ground.

Win the first one if you can. But it’s the second ball that often makes the difference.

#884. League One clubs aim for further curbs on spending as budgets continue to spiral

Wage bills in third tier have increased by 15% this season

‘Luxury tax’ and three-year limits on losses considered

League One clubs want to introduce new spending restrictions to reduce losses by limiting investment from owners.

Clubs in the division voted to tighten the rules last summer by reducing spending limits from 60% to 50% of turnover, and removed a staggered approach to owner investment, so that only 50% of equity injections can be spent on squad costs, with the rest assigned to infrastructure projects. Less than six months later many want to go further.

The Guardian has learned that two proposed models are being ­con­sidered: a fixed cap on owner investment or introducing a version of the Premier League’s squad cost rules, with a £1 levy on clubs for every £1 spent above 50% of their revenue. Sporting sanctions would be applied if spending reached 60%, with the money raised from the levy redistri­buted to other clubs in the division.

The move to introduce more spending curbs comes despite a legal challenge to the existing rules from the Professional ­Footballers’ Association, which launched proceedings in August on the grounds that the clubs had failed to abide by the terms of their membership of the ­professional negotiating and consultative committee.

An attempt by League One and League Two to introduce salary caps of £2.5m and £1.5m respectively was withdrawn in 2021 after the PFA took them to an independent arbitration panel.

Discussions over stricter controls have been taking place for some time, but have been given fresh impetus by the publication last month of the State of the Game report. The first piece of work by the ­Independent Football Regulator showed that 94% of clubs in the EFL and National League are loss-making, and that 32 of the 96 would not survive for a month without owner funding.

The changes last summer reduced the percentage of clubs’ income that can be spent on wages, with mana­gers’ salaries included for the first time, but there is a renewed move to reduce losses, which averaged £7.5m per club in League One last season, up from £5.3m the previous season.

One owner said that further regulation was ­necessary because the clubs had shown ­repeatedly that they could not restrain themselves, pointing out that League One wage bills have increased by 15% this season, and that a top-six budget in the division five years ago would now rank in the bottom three.

Reading and Peterborough have long campaigned for tighter spending controls, but face opposition from clubs such as MK Dons and Wycombe, and it is unclear whether any proposal would gain the two-thirds majority required to be introduced.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

A source at another League One club warned that an unintended consequence would be to create a cliff edge in terms of financial resources with the Championship, which loosened its regulations last season by permitting owners an inject up to £33m over three years, an equity allowance that does not count towards the 85% wage spending/revenue limit.

League Two clubs are also involved in the discussions, although it is unclear whether they will choose to align with League One.

The EFL confirmed discussions were ongoing, although formal proposals have yet to be put to the clubs.

#883. Ben Stiller Reveals Why He's More Protective of His Kids Than Ever

Ben Stiller reflected on his "protective" parenting style for his and his wife Christine Taylor's kids Ella and Quinn in an exclusive E! News interview at the Focker In-Law world premiere.

Ben Stiller isn't focking around when it comes to his kids.

The actor admitted that as his and wife Christine Taylor's kids Ella Stiller, 24, and Quinlin Stiller, 21, have gotten older, he's found himself following the path of his now-overbearing Focker In-Law character Greg Focker.

"I always was more of a Greg guy in terms of, I didn't have a lot of rules and stuff like that," Stiller exclusively told E! News at the movie's world premiere on Nov. 11. "But then, as you let them out into the world, they live their lives, you care about them, you see things coming at them, and you want to be protective.

Similar to Greg's own arc, however, he added, "You try to hold back, too."

Focker In-Law—premiering in theaters Nov. 25—follows Greg as his now-adult son Henry (Skyler Gisondo) brings home his girlfriend Olivia (Ariana Grande) for the first time. More than 25 years after Greg had to impress his now-wife Pam's retired CIA agent/veteran dad Jack Byrnes (Robert De Niro) in Meet the Parents, the tables have turned.

"I understand the Jack Byrnes tendencies, which are similar, honestly, to the Greg [Focker] ones," Stiller posited, "which are to be protective. It's just different ways of expressing it."

After all, while Greg was competing with Olivia—life coach and former FBI hostage negotiator—to establish dominance while riding bikes, Jack strapped her for a polygraph test.

But when it came to working with Grande, Stiller was so into welcoming her to the Focker family.

"She just has amazing timing," he recalled. "She's really, really good. I'd seen her in Wicked, and I knew she was great at doing a very specific kind of character. In this movie, she really pulled something off in creating this person who you're wondering about."

"You're not necessarily rooting for her, but then you are rooting for her," he continued, "because she is a good person, but she's also kind of interesting, too. She gave it all these great colors and she was amazing."

Meanwhile, the Zoolander star admitted he can't quite relax when he reunited with De Niro—with whom he starred in 2000's Meet the Parents, 2004's Meet the Fockers and Little Fockers in 2010—once again.

"Over the years, we've gotten to know each other a little bit, but not that well," he admitted, but teased, "Enough that I'm still intimidated when I see him. I feel like that's always gonna be there. That's part of the dynamic."

But even blue steel wasn't strong enough to calm his nerves while working with the Oscar winner.

"It's always a little something because he's always Robert De Niro," Stiller emphasized. "He is a living legend for us actors."

Now, keep reading to see more of Stiller and Taylor's really, really, really ridiculously good-looking family moments.

Married since 2000, Ben Stiller and wife Christine Taylor broke up in 2017. However, they never filed for divorce. And after to quarantining together with their kids Ella and Quinlin during the pandemic, they reconciled for good.

Ella has often accompanied her father to events over the years, joining Stiller at the June 2023 Tribeca Film Festival debut of the short film Let Liv, which her mom also starred in. For the outing, the trio coordinated in different black outfits.

Previously, Ella served as her dad's plus-one at the 2022 Emmys, the 2018 premiere of Free Solo, the 2017 premiere of The Meyerowitz Stories and the opening night of the Broadway musical Groundhog Day.

In 2019, the duo went to the 2019 Golden Globes together to support Escape to Dannemora, the Showtime miniseries that earned Stiller a nomination for Outstanding Directing.

"I was very happy it went well," the Zoolander actor told E! News of working with Ella. "She showed me a lot of respect, which I appreciated because with a teenage daughter you want to be like, 'Don't be like how we are at home! Let's pretend we're actually nice to each other!' No, it was really a super positive experience for both of us."

In addition to her small role in Escape to Dannemora, Ella has also made appearances in Hubie Halloween and Night at the Museum: Secret of the Tomb.

As Stiller told E! in 2019, Ella "seems to have a desire to explore" an acting career.

Taylor also spoke about Ella's decision, telling Us Weekly in 2018 that she never "discouraged" her from following in her parents' footsteps.

"She came out of the womb with a mission, and I was never going to get in her way," The Brady Bunch Movie alum explained. "She is a very strong-minded, strong-willed young lady, and she loves it. Obviously she was born into the world, but I think living in New York City, she has been exposed to so many incredible things and shows and so … she has the bug. There's nothing you can do about it, but I did not encourage it."

Stiller previously revealed that Ella had a conversation with him about "not being there" during her childhood due to his career.

"She's pretty articulate about it, and sometimes it's stuff that I don't want to hear. It's hard to hear," he explained to Esquire. "Because it's me not being there in the ways that I saw my parents [actors Jerry Stiller and Anne Meara] not being there. I had always thought, 'Well, I won't do that.'"

While Stiller noted that it "didn't feel great" to hear Ella say that, he said it was "important to acknowledge" her feelings: "But then it's that thing that, like, I was trying to navigate my own desire to fulfill the hopes and dreams I had, too."

The Severance director went on to say that Ella and her brother Quinlin were never keeping notes on his absences due to work, they just wanted to spend quality time with their dad.

"What I've learned is that your kids are not keeping score on your career," he explained. "It would be solipsistic to think that my kids actually care about that. They just want a parent who's emotionally present and supportive of them. That's probably what they want more than for me to be going off and pushing the bounds of my creativity."

During an appearance on The Late Show With Stephen Colbert, Stiller revealed Ella had turned him into a major Taylor Swift fan after she made him listen to the singer while he was teaching her how to drive.

"What really helped her was if we just played her favorite artist on the iPhone, and we just played Taylor Swift," he explained. "I was a fan, but I think now I'm a total Swiftie."

Swift's music "would calm her, and it would calm me," Stiller shared before going on to prove just how big of a fan he's become. "We got into the later stuff—Folklore, Evermore. 'Cardigan,' 'Betty' and 'August' all being about the same love triangle but from different points of view. And the characters are named after Ryan Reynolds' and Blake Lively's kids. And then the 'All Too Well' 10-minute Taylor's version from the vault."

After filming Tropic Thunder with Stiller in 2007, Taylor chose to take a break from acting to focus on raising their kids.

"It never felt like a big decision for me," she shared during an appearance on The Morning Call in 2010. "When I had Ella, my whole world changed. I couldn't believe how much love I had for this little creature. I wanted to be a part of it all. I didn't want to miss anything, and with Ben working as much as he does, I felt it was important for one of us to be the stability in the family."

Stiller told Parade in 2016 that he felt "very fortunate" that Taylor made that decision.

Stiller and Taylor decided to adopt a plant-based lifestyle more than a decade ago and inspired their kids to do the same.

CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — NASA has officially launched the Moon Base Student Challenge, asking students to help build humanity's future on the moon. And there's $1 million in prizes up for grabs for the winners.

To build and sustain a base on the moon, NASA will have to solve a myriad of problems. And they're looking to the next generation for help, the space agency's chief Jared Isaacman said Sunday (Nov. 8).

"We are inviting students from across the country to help solve some of the problems that stand between humanity and a permanent presence on another world," Isaacman said. "We're putting 1 million in prizes together to support the best ideas and recognize the teams behind them."

Isaacman made this announcement wearing his blue flight suit from the rocket garden at NASA's Kennedy Space Center Visitor Center amidst the agency's MAX POWER air show event. Just the day before, he flew fighter jets in that suit and even jumped out of a plane, skydiving into the event. Soon after this announcement, he was flying another fighter plane above the crowd.

The audience for this announcement was filled with students of all ages. Some young children wearing costume spacesuits squeezed as close as they could to the front of the room while teenagers considering their futures listened intently. It was clear that Isaacman's presence and words were landing with this group.

But what moon base challenges does NASA want to see these students tackle? In short, all of them.

"The moon base will allow us to conduct groundbreaking science, test new technologies, and prepare again for where we inevitably go next, which is the red planet," he said. "But before any of that can happen, we have an awful lot of problems that need to be solved."

"We need ways to generate power through the long lunar night. We need to protect our astronauts from that incredibly harsh and dangerous and demanding environment on the surface. We need to move people and equipment around on the surface and support human life three days away from Earth," Isaacman said, illustrating just a few of the big issues that present with the concept of a moon base.

This challenge is open to high school and post-secondary students based in the U.S. For participating students, they will form teams that will work on an idea from one of six different technical topics related to creating and running a moon base. These six topics include power systems, habitats, communications, mobility, life support and astronaut safety.

This will be what Isaacman described as a "multi-phase competition that mirrors how ideas are developed actually in the aerospace industry."

"Teams will first submit concepts, then they're going to refine them, and finalists will have the opportunity to present their solutions directly to NASA leaders and stakeholders," he further explained.

"The prize money is great for sure, but the the real opportunity is to work on problems NASA is actively trying to solve right now, so students don't need to wait to graduation to contribute to that effort," Isaacman added.

Right now, NASA has a long road ahead of them before a moon base is actually built. In mid-2027, the agency is planning to launch its Artemis III mission which will see a crew of four astronauts practice rendezvous maneuvers with two different lunar landers. If all goes to plan, this will be followed by Artemis IV landing humans on the moon's surface for the first time since the final Apollo mission in 1972.

The agency is making these big steps forward to not just a crewed return to the moon, but a sustained, long-term return to the moon. However, knowing that a fully-fledged moon base is still firmly in the future, they are banking on the ingenuity, creativity and passion of

If you're a student or know a student interested in participating in this challenge, you can find more information on NASA's website here. Interested students can register until Jan. 25, 2027.

#879. US withdraw from U-17 World Cup in Qatar due to safety concerns

USSF cites state department advisory about Qatar

Competition set to kick off in eight days

The US men’s national team have pulled out of the Fifa U-17 World Cup, which is due to kick off in Qatar in just over a week. In a letter sent to players explaining the decision, the US Soccer Federation cited safety concerns for players and staff, referring them to the US state department’s travel advisory for Qatar, which encourages citizens to reconsider travel to the country “due to risk of armed conflict” and asks government employees to obtain special authorization to do so.

“Unfortunately, in light of current circumstances … we are no longer able to participate in the tournament,” US Soccer’s letter to players reads. “The wellbeing of our players and staff will always be our top priority.

“Please accept our deepest appreciation for your commitment to US Soccer and our shared disappointment about these circumstances.”

A US Soccer spokesperson said the federation would not go into details about how it reached its decision. The Guardian understands Fifa was informed of the federation’s decision on Wednesday.

Fifa’s regulations for the U-17 World Cups stipulate that qualified nations must participate in the tournament or be fined, with withdrawal within 30 days of the tournament’s start resulting in a fine of CHF20,000 (about $24,000).

“Fifa has been informed of US Soccer’s decision to withdraw from the Fifa U-17 World Cup Qatar 2026,” Fifa told the Guardian in a statement. “The applicable tournament regulations will be followed. Fifa’s security assessments remain unchanged, and no new developments affecting the security situation around the tournament have occurred. Fifa understands that US Soccer’s decision was made in light of the existing US Level 3 travel advisory.”

The ongoing situation in the Middle East – involving interconnected conflicts among multiple states – has already led to postponements or cancellations of international sporting events. The 2027 Asian Cup, the continental soccer championship, was due to be held in Saudi Arabia in January 2027 but has been postponed nearly a year due to the conflict between the Saudis and the Houthi rebels, and the Iran war. More recently, Qatar pulled out of hosting rugby’s 2028 Nations Championship finals due to uncertainty around the conflicts. The final races of the Formula One season are still going ahead in the Middle East, on 29 November in Qatar and then 6 December in Abu Dhabi.

Fifa told the Guardian it had taken the situation in the Middle East into account.

“The safety and security of all participants and fans remains paramount,” Fifa said in its statement. “As with all Fifa tournaments and events, we are in close contact with the relevant authorities and are looking forward to the tournament kick-off in Qatar. In recent months, Qatar has successfully hosted several international events, including the FIP Padel World Cup, the FIVB Volleyball Boys’ U17 World Championship, the Doha Diamond League, the Fiba Basketball World Cup 2027 Asian Qualifiers, the MotoGP and the UN ITU PP.”

Jude Bellingham shared an old photo of him and brother Jobe after England's squad announcement last week

It is six years since Jude Bellingham played his final game for Birmingham City, and three years since younger brother Jobe wore the club's shirt for the last time.

While Jude, 23, is establishing himself as a footballing great at European greats Real Madrid following a spell at Borussia Dortmund, Jobe, 21, is continuing his football education at his brother's former club in Germany after two seasons with Sunderland.

The Stourbridge-born midfielders have moved on with their careers.

Their memories, however, live on at St Andrew's, such was the impact the boyhood Birmingham fans made in the Championship.

On match days supporters stop and pose for photographs in front of Jude's mural outside the ground. Fans still turn up to matches wearing Bellingham shirts.

"They both had a real connection with fans," Craig Courtney, from the Tilton Talk fan podcast, told BBC Sport. "Fans loved the fact they both cared.

"They wore their hearts on their sleeves and helped Birmingham when we were fighting relegation. Even now, Jude and Jobe remember where it all started for them."

The brothers played 70 league and cup games between them for Birmingham after graduating from the academy.

They have never appeared together in a senior match, however, as Jude - who joined Birmingham aged eight - had left by the time Jobe broke into the first team in 2022.

The Bellinghams will become the first brothers to play for England for 19 years if Jobe wins his first cap and appears alongside Jude, a veteran of 60 appearances, in the Nations League game with Croatia at Wembley.

"It will be an incredibly proud moment for Birmingham City if that happens," said Courtney.

'A beautiful story' as Bellingham brothers called up

Listen: How Jude Bellingham became a global brand

Birmingham supporters have had little to cheer about recently.

It is 15 years since they last appeared in the Premier League, while the 2011 League Cup winners even dipped down to League One recently.

While fierce rivals Aston Villa were playing - and beating - Bayern Munich and Bologna in the Champions League two years ago, Birmingham were losing at Shrewsbury and drawing with Northampton Town.

After 15 games Birmingham sit top of the Championship and there are plans for a new 62,000-capacity stadium in time for 2030-31.

"As a club, we've been right down in the doldrums," added Courtney. "Now we're top of the table and having a new stadium built.

"There is an argument that none of this would have been possible without the fees received for Jude and Jobe."

A mural tribute to Jude Bellingham outside St Andrew's

Jude is the youngest player in Birmingham's history after making his debut aged 16 years and 38 days in 2019.

Clubs across Europe were pursuing him when he signed his first professional contact in 2020 after turning 17 - a deal both he and Birmingham knew would never be fulfilled.

His actions, however, ensured Birmingham would receive a significant transfer fee when he left, and soon afterwards he joined Dortmund for an initial fee of Â£20m during the Covid-19 pandemic.

When he joined Real in 2023, Birmingham received a reported sell-on fee of at least Â£10m., external

"We cannot possibly imagine, without Jude's decision [to sign a contract], where we would be as a club in a pandemic like this," then Birmingham chief executive Xuandong Ren told BBC WM after Jude joined Dortmund.

"He could easily have just looked after himself and not the club, but he chose the best possible way to look after the club."

Jobe became the second youngest player to play for Birmingham when he made his debut in January 2022 aged 16 years and 107 days.

"This was a lad, regardless of who his brother was or what he was achieving, who would do anything to write his own success story," former Birmingham striker Troy Deeney, who played in the game when Jobe made his debut, told the Sun., external

"Everything he has achieved on the pitch, too, has come with an instant comparison to his older brother.

"He never got that one moment to enjoy something without someone, somewhere saying: 'Yeah, but what about Jude?'

"That only added to how strong he was mentally, and anyone who suggests he is where he is because of his last name is talking rubbish."

Deeney added: "What impressed me more than anything he had done on the pitch was his attitude - a hell-bent determination to get to the top and the common sense to take all the right steps along the way."

Jobe played 26 games before Sunderland paid Â£3m for him in 2023, with Birmingham receiving a reported Â£4m sell-on fee when he moved to Dortmund two years later.

Although significantly less than the fees generated by his brother, it was nevertheless welcome revenue.

Jobe Bellingham was given his Birmingham City debut by manager Lee Bowyer in January 2022

Both Jude and Jobe have returned to St Andrew's since their transfers.

Jobe captained England Under-21s to a 2-0 win against the Republic of Ireland at his old ground last November.

Before that match U21s boss Lee Carsley, who managed Jude when he was England interim manager in 2024, praised the brothers for their work ethic and determination to be the best.

Carsley said: "I know how much they love the Blues still and how important the club is to them."

Jude, tipped to be a future England captain, was at St Andrew's in July watching his former club in a pre-season friendly against Barcelona. He even wore a Birmingham shirt while watching from the stands.

Jude wore a Birmingham City shirt when he returned to St Andrew's

When Jude joined Dortmund in 2020 Birmingham retired the 17-year-old's number 22 shirt after 44 appearances.

"That was a gesture of thanks for what Jude had done," said Courtney.

"It might be wishful thinking, but I really believe Jude has unfinished business at Birmingham. I can see a scenario before he retires where he gets an opportunity to wear the number 22 again."

Should the Bellingham brothers play together against Croatia, they will become the first siblings to appear for England since Gary and Phil Neville against Spain in a friendly at Old Trafford in 2007.

It will be an immensely proud moment for their parents, Mark and Denise.

"We've played together for so long in the street and to play with my brother Jobe for England would be the biggest dream of my life," Jude, a Champions League and La Liga winner with Real Madrid, wrote on social media, external in 2024.

"That would mean more than any of the trophies. Nothing would even get close to that... nothing."

BBC reporter John Watson has been finding out why Bellingham is proving so popular with football fans across the world
