The Seestar S30 Plus is a great beginner smart telescope for deep-sky imaging, along with a reasonable price tag and enough features to develop your astro skills without buying another instrument.

Excellent deep-sky imaging, even with light pollution

Built-in filters and easy automated set-up

Lower resolution than more expensive smart telescopes

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

I’ve used several smart telescopes over the last few years, but I'd recommend the ZWO Seestar S30 Plus to almost anyone wanting to get started in astrophotography. At $499/€499, it’s a complete imaging system that can photograph galaxies, nebulae and star clusters automatically, even from a light-polluted city. Better still, it’s so small that it can live on a bookshelf.

I recently captured images of the Dumbbell Nebula (M27), the North America Nebula (NGC 7000), the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) and the Pleiades (M45) with the S30 Plus. All were remarkably easy to capture, and none of the images accompanying this review required external processing. It’s basically point-and-shoot astrophotography — if you live under light-polluted skies, that’s a game-changer.

I also think the S30 Plus makes an ideal companion to a conventional optical telescope. I can set it to photograph a nebula I have no hope of seeing under light pollution while I try to find brighter objects through the eyepiece of another telescope. It will then get on with collecting photons while I enjoy observing.

For anyone who already owns a telescope but doesn’t want the expense and complexity of conventional astrophotography, that’s a compelling proposition.

One problem with buying a cheap optical telescope is that deep-sky objects rarely resemble the colorful photographs you see online. The moon, planets and bright star clusters can look wonderful through an eyepiece, but faint galaxies and nebulas are much harder to appreciate, particularly from a town or city.

Like all smart telescopes, the S30 Plus gets around that problem by photographing objects rather than showing them directly. Its camera takes repeated exposures, which the telescope automatically stacks to reduce noise and gradually reveal faint detail. The longer you leave it working, the better the resulting image tends to become.

Being able to photograph colorful nebulas without traveling to a remote observing site is one of the biggest attractions of the S30 Plus. For beginners living in cities, it could transform their experience of astronomy.

I’ve always preferred spending my nights looking at the sky rather than fiddling with equipment, which is one reason I enjoy smart telescopes. Traditional astrophotography can involve a camera, tracking mount, adapters, cables, alignment, a laptop and considerable patience before the first useful exposure begins. The S30 Plus removes almost all of that.

I can put it outside, connect the Seestar app and choose a target from its built-in sky atlas. The telescope then moves to the correct position, identifies the star field, centers the object, focuses and begins imaging. Within minutes, a photograph starts appearing on my smartphone. That leaves me free to use an optical telescope alongside it — or stay inside and do something else.

Using the S30 Plus’s built-in UV/IR cut filter — which blocks ultraviolet and infrared light — I captured the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), a popular deep-sky object. As the hours went by, the dust lanes on its outskirts appeared in ever more detail. That’s how smart telescopes work — they collect and combine dozens or hundreds of short exposures, gradually revealing fainter structure while reducing noise.

So impressive is the image after only about five or six exposures that it’s tempting to stop after a few minutes — but patience makes an enormous difference. Fortunately, you don’t have to stand beside the S30 Plus. You can leave it collecting light — even overnight, thanks to its scheduling option (though it’s not waterproof, so check the weather forecast!).

Using the dual-band anti-light pollution filter, the Pleiades open cluster (M45) provided another interesting test. The S30 Plus has a mosaic mode that photographs overlapping sections of sky to create a larger image than its main camera can capture in a single frame. It’s ideal for expansive targets such as the Pleiades and Andromeda, although gathering enough exposures takes time. The app shows how much of the mosaic has been completed, and if needs be, you can continue collecting data on subsequent nights.

I also photographed the Double Cluster in Perseus (NGC 869 and NGC 884) and the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules (M13), both relatively swift targets, but as anyone who’s used a smart telescope knows, it’s the faint nebulas that are the real prize. For those, dark skies mean better data — and that’s exactly why a smart telescope needs to be portable.

The S30 Plus weighs just 3.64 lbs (1.65 kg) and measures 8.25 x 5.5 x 3.15 inches (210 x 140 x 80 mm) when switched off. That’s small enough to fit into a camera bag in place of another lens or camera body, which is a major advantage because I travel to remote locations quite frequently. That fact that it sits on such a tiny tripod is also a boon.

I’ve recently used the much larger Seestar S50 Pro, which weighs 6.17 lbs (2.8 kg). It’s a more capable imaging instrument with a 50mm aperture and a larger 8.3-megapixel sensor, but its heavier, bulkier chassis is harder to get into carry-on luggage. The S30 Plus and the higher-spec S30 Pro also differ from the S50 Pro in that they come with a padded carry case. This has a useful carrying handle, although there’s no shoulder strap or dedicated storage for the tripod and magnetic solar filter.

It’s also worth taking along a portable battery and USB-C cable to recharge its built-in 6,000mAh battery during long sessions, though it lasts about six hours, which will suit most observing sessions.

The original, now-discontinued S30 was already impressive, but the S30 Plus is a substantial upgrade. It has improved four-element apochromatic optics with ED glass and two 3.7-megapixel cameras, each producing 1,440x2,560-pixel images. That’s almost 80% more pixels than the original S30’s main camera.

The main camera’s field of view has increased slightly to about three degrees, while the wide-angle camera now covers 43.5 degrees of sky. The latter can be used for star trails, though I suspect it’s something most people will experiment with occasionally.

There’s also an EQ mode. This will align the telescope with Earth’s rotation to allow longer exposures and sharper edges, which I found worked really well. It requires an appropriately angled mount or wedge (such as the Seestar TH10 Fluid Tripod Head) and a small tripod.

I tested it at 51 degrees north, which randomly appears to be the cut-off point for ease of use because of the tilt it puts on the telescope. It’s when a tripod begins to topple with the weight, meaning you need a tripod whose legs can be set at a low angle (Seestar’s TC20 tripod would be ideal, and is very compact).

The app makes it all very easy to set up, and advanced imaging possibilities like this are welcome. So, too, is the option of outputting images as lossless FITS files for anyone wanting to process their images using specialist software.

That’s what makes the Seestar S30 Plus such a good beginner’s telescope. It’s easy to use immediately, but there’s plenty of scope to develop more sophisticated astrophotography skills without buying another instrument.

The S30 Plus isn’t limited to deep-sky photography. I photographed a near-full moon against a blue daytime sky, something I particularly enjoy doing with smart telescopes because they’re so quick to set up.

It also comes with a magnetic white-light solar filter, allowing safe photographs of the sun when the filter is securely fitted. This must always be installed before pointing the telescope towards the sun. I did have to manually guide the S30 Plus to the sun and moon on a few occasions, but it’s easy enough to do, and I actually like the option to manually take control — few other smart telescopes allow it. Once you’ve found the sun or moon, the scope centers it and keeps it in view (unless you’re on a moving ship, by the way, where tracking generally fails — something for eclipse chasers to think about).

Planetary photography is less impressive. The 30mm aperture and short focal length aren’t ideal for detailed views of Jupiter or Saturn, so for anyone primarily interested in observing and imaging planets, I’d recommend a conventional optical telescope instead.

The S30 Plus occupies an interesting position in ZWO’s increasingly crowded Seestar range. With dual 8.3MP cameras and wider fields of view, the S30 Pro is a worthy upgrade from the original S30. Meanwhile, the $999 S50 Pro has a larger 50mm aperture that collects almost three times as much light, although it’s also significantly bulkier and more expensive.

Alternatives exist outside ZWO’s range. DwarfLab’s Dwarf Mini is exceptionally portable, but its lower resolution and more limited capabilities make it less versatile. At the other extreme, Unistellar’s Odyssey has an 85mm aperture, an electronic eyepiece and opportunities to contribute to citizen science projects, but it sits in a different price bracket.

The S30 Plus will hit the sweet spot for many. It offers almost everything a beginner needs to explore deep-sky astrophotography, with built-in filters, mosaic mode and EQ tracking giving plenty of advanced features to grow into. Crucially, it’s small enough to travel with easily. Yes, you can spend more and get slightly better image data, but most beginners don’t need to.

The Seestar S30 Plus is one of the most affordable smart telescopes available, but it’s also one of the best-value offerings in its class.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#778. Rubin Observatory discovers two hidden companions of the Milky Way. Hundreds more may be waiting

The powerful new Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile has already uncovered two previously unknown companions of the Milky Way, offering an early glimpse of what could become a much larger wave of discoveries. Astronomers believe hundreds of faint galaxies may still be hiding around our galaxy, and the observatory could finally bring many of them into view.

Located on Cerro Pachón in the Chilean Andes, the recently completed NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory is designed to explore the sky in extraordinary detail. Its initial observations have now revealed two elusive objects that had escaped detection, demonstrating the telescope's ability to find some of the faintest members of our galactic neighborhood.

Large galaxies such as the Milky Way are surrounded by smaller companions known as satellites. These include dwarf galaxies and star clusters, many of which contain so few stars that they are extremely difficult to detect. Astronomers have identified approximately 65 satellite galaxies around the Milky Way, but some estimates suggest that hundreds more remain undiscovered.

Two new studies, including one led by a Yale astronomer, suggest that Rubin could play a major role in finding these missing objects and completing the picture of our galaxy's surroundings.

Two Hidden Companions of the Milky Way Discovered

Using observations collected before the observatory's official launch, researchers identified two exceptionally faint satellites that had never been seen before.

The first, Aquarius IV, is a tiny galaxy located in the distant outskirts of the Milky Way, approximately 355,000 light-years from Earth. The second, Rubin-GC1, is a star cluster on the opposite side of our galaxy, hidden within a region where thick clouds of cosmic dust make observations especially challenging.

Both discoveries are remarkable because astronomers made them using only a small amount of the data Rubin is expected to collect over its lifetime.

"What I find especially exciting is that these discoveries are just the beginning for Rubin," said William Cerny, an astronomy student in Yale's Graduate School of Arts and Sciences.

Cerny is the lead author of the Aquarius IV study, published in Research Notes of the AAS, and the second author of the Rubin-GC1 study, which has been accepted by The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

"If the observatory can find systems this faint and difficult with only its preview data, its full 10-year survey will undoubtedly provide us with many more Milky Way satellite discoveries," Cerny said. "These new satellites will give us new opportunities to test models of galaxy formation, trace the assembly history of the Milky Way, and investigate the nature of dark matter."

A Powerful New Telescope Is Just Getting Started

Rubin began its ambitious 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) in June. The project aims to produce an exceptionally detailed record of the changing night sky while searching for objects that previous telescopes have been unable to detect.

One of its major scientific goals is to map the Milky Way's "halo," a vast, roughly spherical region that surrounds the galaxy's main disk. This halo contains scattered stars, gas, and dark matter, along with faint satellite galaxies, star clusters, and other structures that preserve clues about the Milky Way's past.

To carry out this enormous survey, Rubin uses the 8.4-meter Simonyi Survey Telescope and the largest digital camera ever constructed, capable of capturing images with 3.2 gigapixels of resolution. By repeatedly photographing large areas of the Southern Hemisphere sky, the observatory will build an extraordinarily wide-ranging time-lapse record of the universe.

The facility is jointly funded by the National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science.

Just 7% of the Night Sky Revealed Two New Satellites

For the new studies, astronomers examined preview observations gathered between April 2025 and January 2026. These images covered only about 7% of the entire night sky, yet they were sufficient to reveal two previously unknown companions of the Milky Way.

The discoveries offer an encouraging indication of what could emerge as Rubin continues collecting data across a much larger portion of the sky.

"Finding new Milky Way satellites in Rubin Observatory data has been an exciting future prospect for most of my career," said Marla Geha, a professor of astronomy and physics in Yale's Faculty of Arts and Sciences, and co-author on both studies. "It is remarkable this is now a reality."

The research involved a broad international collaboration. In addition to Yale, participating institutions included the University of Chicago, the University of Virginia, the University of Washington, Dartmouth College, the University of Tampa, NSF NOIRLab, Duke University, the University of Toronto, the Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucía in Spain, the University of Colorado-Boulder, and Lund University in Sweden.

Aashay Pai of the University of Chicago served as the first author of the study describing Rubin-GC1.

Hidden Galaxies Could Reveal New Clues About Dark Matter

Finding additional satellites could do much more than expand the known population of galaxies surrounding the Milky Way. These faint objects may also help astronomers investigate one of the universe's greatest mysteries: dark matter.

Dark matter is an invisible form of matter that does not emit or reflect light, making it impossible to observe directly with conventional telescopes. Scientists infer its existence from the gravitational effects it produces on stars, galaxies, and other cosmic structures. It accounts for most of the matter in the universe and provides much of the gravitational framework that holds galaxies together.

Ultra-faint galaxies such as Aquarius IV are particularly valuable for studying dark matter. They contain only a small fraction of the stars found in larger galaxies, yet dark matter dominates their total mass. By examining their properties and movements, researchers can test ideas about how dark matter behaves and influences the formation of galaxies.

These discoveries could also help scientists reconstruct the Milky Way's long history. The positions, motions, and properties of small satellite galaxies can reveal how larger galaxies assembled over billions of years, including how they accumulated matter and interacted with smaller systems.

Rubin's early findings may also provide important clues about how the universe's smallest and faintest galaxies form, evolve, and survive.

"These discoveries are incredibly promising," Geha said. "Continued discoveries will allow us to complete the census of satellite galaxies around the Milky Way, which is a key to understanding how the faintest galaxies form."

#777. Sienna Spiro Cancels Appearance at 2026 ARIA Awards: ‘I Have to Listen to My Body’

Melbourne-based hyperpop trio Blusher will take Spiro's spot in the line-up for the the 40th annual ARIAs.

Sienna Spiro won’t be making the trip to Australia next week, as planned, where she was expected to perform at the 2026 ARIA Awards.

The rising British singer and songwriter pulls out of the 40th annual awards ceremony, due to the physical demands of her latest tour.

“I am so incredibly sorry I won’t be able to make it to the ARIA Awards this year,” she writes in a post, shared on ARIA’s Instagram Stories. “I’ve been looking forward to coming back for months, however this tour has taken its toll on me and my voice.”

Spiro recently completed the North American run of the My House World Tour, in support of her hit debut album, Visitor. Explore Blusher Sienna Spiro See latest videos, charts and news

“As much as I wanted to be there,” her statement continues, “I have to listen to my body and give it the rest it needs to be able to give you the best shows possible when I return in January.” Related Aria Vega Wins Best New Artist at the 2026 Latin Grammys: 'Dreams Know No Fear' On Winning First Latin Grammy, Camila Fernández Thanks Expectant Baby for 'Strength to be Here' 50 Cent Trolls Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's Affair With 'P.I.M.P.' Music Video AI Deepfake: 'Jensen Don't Sweat It'

Spiro was the first international performer announced for this year’s ARIAs, to be presented Wednesday, Nov. 18 at Sydney’s Hordern Pavilion. In years past, the ARIAs has booked the likes of Billie Eilish, Dua Lipa, Ed Sheeran, One Direction, Robbie Williams, Taylor Swift and Olivia Dean, who has been a force on the ARIA Charts ever since her performance at the 2025 edition.

Her trip to the ARIAs was meant to be Spiro’s second trip to Australia following an intimate fan event last year at Pleasure Club in Newtown, Sydney. She’ll return in January 2027 for her eight-date My House Tour of Australia and New Zealand, which includes two nights at the Hordern. The trek sold out in a matter of hours, according to promoter Frontier Touring.

“I am incredibly grateful to the ARIA team for the opportunity and so sad to let you all down,” she writes.

At just 21 years of age, the Londoner has already accumulated more than 36 million monthly listeners on Spotify, headline sponsor of the ARIAs, and upwards of 2 billion total streams; bagged three simultaneous Billboard Hot 100 singles; and six entries on the ARIA Singles Chart. “Die On This Hill” is certified platinum by ARIA, while “You Stole The Show,” “MAYBE,” “Material Lover” and “The Visitor” are all certified Gold in these parts.

In her place, Atlantic Records-signed, Melbourne-based hyperpop trio Blusher will join the line up for the ARIAs, reads a statement from the trade body, for what will “be an unforgettable night honoring four decades of Australian music.”

With eight nominations each, Tame Impala and Genesis Owusu lead the pack for the 40th annual ARIA Awards, while Ecca Vandal, winner of the 2026 Australian Music Prize, is close behind with seven nods.

The 2026 ARIA Awards is supported by Destination NSW, in partnership with Spotify, and will be live on Paramount+ and broadcast on 10. Performances and moments will also be available on the @ARIA.official YouTube channel.

#775. NASA is racing against time to save the Hubble Space Telescope

NASA is investigating whether private space companies could help extend the life of the Hubble Space Telescope, which has spent more than 35 years transforming our understanding of the universe.

On October 29, the agency issued a Request for Information seeking details about commercial technologies that could be used to service Hubble while it remains in orbit. The goal is to determine whether new spacecraft capabilities could keep the iconic observatory operating longer, improve its performance, or help bring its mission to a safe conclusion.

"Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already on orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble's life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the universe."

NASA Considers Raising Hubble Into a Higher Orbit

One possibility under consideration is sending a spacecraft to push Hubble into a higher orbit. This could counteract the gradual loss of altitude that threatens the telescope's future and potentially allow it to continue making scientific discoveries for additional years.

NASA is also interested in missions that could service the telescope and improve its capabilities. Another option would focus on safely retiring Hubble when its scientific work is complete, either by guiding it through a controlled descent into Earth's atmosphere or arranging for its disposal in orbit.

These possibilities are being explored rather than formally approved. By reaching out to commercial companies, NASA hopes to better understand what technologies are available and whether they could provide practical, affordable solutions.

"Hubble is a national icon that has fundamentally changed how humanity views our universe for more than 35 years," said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. "Commercial industry has rapidly evolved in recent years to offer new capabilities for in-space satellite capture and servicing. Given the time we have until Hubble's anticipated re-entry, we are eager to explore the breadth of possibilities to boost Hubble to a higher orbit while we develop the flagship mission to follow."

Companies interested in participating can review NASA's Request for Information online. The agency is accepting responses until 3 p.m. EST on Monday, November 30.

Why Hubble Could Fall Back to Earth by 2034

Although Hubble continues to operate in space, its orbit is gradually shrinking. The telescope travels through low Earth orbit, where traces of Earth's atmosphere create drag that slowly reduces the altitude of orbiting spacecraft.

Even hundreds of miles above the planet, the atmosphere is not completely absent. The tiny amount of remaining gas produces resistance as spacecraft move through it. Over long periods, this effect can cause satellites to lose altitude and eventually descend into denser layers of the atmosphere.

Unlike spacecraft equipped with engines that can periodically raise their orbits, Hubble has no propulsion system capable of maintaining its altitude. Without outside assistance, it cannot reverse this gradual orbital decline.

NASA's current analysis suggests that Hubble will likely reenter Earth's atmosphere sometime between 2033 and 2034. To prevent that outcome through an orbital boost, the agency expects that a mission would need to occur by 2032.

That timeline leaves a limited window to evaluate potential solutions, develop a mission, and carry it out before the telescope descends too far.

Extending Hubble's Legacy of Cosmic Discoveries

Since beginning operations more than three decades ago, Hubble has become one of the most influential scientific observatories ever launched. Its observations have helped reshape astronomers' understanding of the cosmos, and the telescope continues to produce discoveries that advance research across many areas of astronomy.

Hubble is also the product of a longstanding international partnership between NASA and ESA (European Space Agency).

NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, oversees the telescope and its mission operations, with additional operational support from Denver-based Lockheed Martin Space.

Scientific operations are handled by the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, which is operated by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy on NASA's behalf.

With commercial spaceflight technology advancing, NASA is now evaluating whether Hubble could benefit from capabilities that were not available when it was originally designed. A successful mission to raise its orbit or enhance its systems could allow the historic telescope to continue exploring the universe well beyond its currently projected orbital lifetime.

Materials provided by NASA. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#774. Rosalía and Milo J Sweep the 2026 Latin Grammys: Full List of Winners

CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso, Jorge Drexler, Karol G and Grupo Frontera also won multiple awards on Thursday's (Nov. 12) ceremony.

With her widely acclaimed and eclectic LUX, Rosalía won the Latin Grammy for album of the year for the third time and took home, among other honors, song of the year for “La Perla,” alongside Yahritza y Su Esencia. It was an expected victory on a night that honored both major icons and fresh new voices of Latin music — such as Milo J, the Argentine newcomer who won the award for record of the year for “Niño” and took home three additional trophies, including best folk music album for La Vida Es Más Corta.

Rosalía also won awards for best pop song and best alternative music album, and LUX was further recognized for its recording engineering. But the honor that moved her to tears was, without a doubt, album of the year, which she received from Juanes — an artist who supported her very early in her career and whom she thanked for being there back when “there were only 100 people in a room in Madrid.”

“This is the third time I’ve won this award. If El Mal Querer was a dream, and Motomami was a bold gamble, then LUX has been a leap into the unknown,” said the Spanish superstar, referring to her winning albums of 2019 and 2022, respectively. “I believe it’s very important to speak your own truth — and for others to be able to speak theirs — and this record is mine. I thank God, and I thank my loved ones — my family and my friends. Thank-you for your love and for shaping me into who I am today. The truth is, I know I still have a lot to learn, and I’m certain that I likely haven’t even created my best work yet.”

Milo J, who at 19 years old earned six nominations for a project that pushed him well outside his comfort zone (urban music), also won for best urban/urban fusion performance for “Gil,” featuring Trueno, as well as for best recording package. He was also a contender for the album of the year award. “Coming from where I come from — from the trap genre — winning an award for folk music just blows my mind,” he said upon receiving the gramophone for best folk album. Milo spoke during the Latin Grammy Premiere — the non-televised ceremony held hours earlier, where the majority of the winners were announced — and used the moment to thank the producers and colleagues who contributed to the project.Among the winners announced during the ceremony, Karol G shone as she received the award for best urban music album for the third time — this time for Tropicoqueta.

“I’m going to be completely honest — thank God I’ve been here a few times before — but making Tropicoqueta meant so much to me, in ways many people can’t even imagine,” the Colombian star said. “I sat down with artists and musical masters I never dreamed I’d have the chance to collaborate or work with. I feel I’ve grown a great deal, both as a person and as an artist. Most importantly, I now have an album that I’m touring with, and when I perform these songs, I can see that people feel proud to be Latino. It’s beautiful to watch everyone singing along to salsa, merengue, reggaeton, bachata and mariachi — because that’s who we are: all of that, and so much more. So, thank-you.”

Among the veteran honorees were Jorge Drexler, Juanes and Fonseca, while first-time winners included the young Mexican artist Xavi and Brazilian superstar Anitta — who secured her first Latin Grammy after 12 nominations, winning best Portuguese language contemporary pop album for Equilibrivm.The coveted best new artist award went to Colombian Aria Vega, who was Billboard’s Latin Up-And-Comer artist of the month for July and recently participated in the Women’s Panel at Billboard Latin Music Week.

“I was reflecting on where I am in my life, and I thought of a college professor who once gave us an assignment to create something that described us. I put together some clippings that read ‘big dreams and good taste.’ Being here to receive this recognition is one of those ‘premium’ dreams,” she said upon accepting her award.

CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso, the sensational Argentine duo that took home five awards during their Latin Grammy debut last year, won best Latin electronic music performance for “Beto’s Horns – Fred Remix” with Fred Again..; best pop/rock song for “Hasta Jesús Tuvo Un Mal Día” with Sting; and best long form music video for FREE SPIRITS (The Film).

Other early winners included Luis Enrique, Grupo Frontera, Camila Fernández and Bobby Pulido — the latter having recently been elected to the House of Representatives for the Democrats.

“I want to tell you that I’m retiring from music, and I’m leaving with so much gratitude,” he said while accepting his trophy. “I’m so, so proud to be from Texas and to be Tejano and to represent this music. Tejano music is in very good hands; we have so much talent — young talent like [fellow nominees] Jay Pérez, Destiny Navaira, everyone who’s here. I love you all, and I’ll see you soon, because we need to represent and we need to get to work to use our voices for something else.”

Among the big surprises of the everning, Venezuelan newcomer Sara Schell took home the award for songwriter of the year, besting heavyweights such as Edgar Barrera — who led the list of nominees with 10 nods and went on to win his fourth producer of the year award.

“I’m shaking—wow,” said the 23-year-old songwriter as she accepted her golden gramophone. “My name is Sara Schell; I’m from Barquisimeto, Venezuela, and this award is for my family. And when I say ‘my family,’ I don’t just mean my mom and dad… I also mean my friends and my team. Thank you for all the support; thank you for all the love.”

Daddy Yankee — the Latin Recording Academy’s 2026 Person of the Year, honored a day before by his peers at a traditional gala — also won best urban song alongside Bizarrap for “Daddy Yankee: Bzrp Music Sessions, Vol. 0/66.”

The 27th Annual Latin Grammy Awards ceremony, hosted by singer and actress Roselyn Sánchez, was broadcast live from Las Vegas on TelevisaUnivision platforms. Performers included Rosalía, Karol G, Anitta, Elena Rose, Juanes, Milo J, Mon Laferte and many others.

#773. Out of space before finals? 5 Sandisk storage upgrades built for campus life

Your phone won't let you record a lecture because the storage is full, your laptop keeps surfacing "manage storage" pop-ups you've been ignoring for weeks, and you finally go to download the game you've been waiting for, only to realize you don't have enough space.

The reflex when a device runs out of room is to assume the device itself is the problem, but the fix is a lot less drastic and a lot less expensive than a replacement. Sandisk has 5 upgrade options, each one designed for a different "I've run out of space" moment.

The SanDisk Phone Drive with USB-C (starting at $112.99) plugs straight into your USB-C smartphone and can add up to 1TB* of extra space, which is enough to keep you from deleting photos from your camera roll in between classes. It moves files between your phone, tablet, and laptop, and other USB-C compatible devices without a cable or cloud upload, and it comes in four colors, so it can stand out from the clutter at the bottom of your bag.

The SANDISK Extreme Fit USB-C Flash Drive (starting at $34.99) uses a "plug-and-stay" design that sits nearly flush with your laptop's USB-C port, so it stays put when you shove the laptop into a backpack and move between classes. With up to 1TB* of extra capacity, there’s plenty of room to offload a semester’s worth of project files and free up space for what you’re working on next.

The SANDISK Portable Drive (starting at $112.99) is a pocket-sized alternative to the bulky portable hard drives of the past, with transfer speeds up to 4x faster than old-school portable hard drives**. Toss it in your backpack to keep the files you want to hang onto close at hand, whether you’re moving between your dorm, the library, class, or heading home for break. It’s an easy way to add everyday storage to your setup and make more room on the devices you already use. Turn your laptop into a gaming rig

The SANDISK Optimus GX 7100 NVMe SSD (starting at $207.99) is the internal upgrade option that installs inside a compatible laptop and adds fast NVMe storage with a power-efficient architecture so that a game library and a semester’s worth of assignments can coexist on one machine. The appeal is simple — upgrade what you already own instead of replacing it.

The SANDISK Optimus GX 7100M NVMe SSD (starting at $387.99) is the handheld version of the same idea, adding up to 2TB* of space to compatible gaming handhelds. With AAA titles routinely running 90GB or more, up to 2TB* means your game library travels with you instead of having to decide which ones make the cut.

Solve your storage problems for good with Sandisk without monthly storage subscription fees. You'll have an easier time getting back into your creative flow, too.

* 1GB=1,000,000,000 bytes. 1TB=1,000,000,000,000 bytes. Actual user storage capacity less.

**  Based on read speed and internal testing against select commercially available 1TB portable HDDs. Performance may vary depending upon host device, usage conditions, drive capacity, and other factors.

SANDISK, the SANDISK logo, SANDISK Extreme, SANDISK Extreme Fit and SANDISK Optimus are registered trademarks or trademarks of Sandisk Corporation or its affiliates in the US and/or other countries. #772. SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism

For nearly 90 years, physicists have divided magnetic materials into two main categories: ferromagnets and antiferromagnets. Now, scientists have confirmed that a third type exists, revealing a previously unrecognized form of magnetic behavior that could lead to major advances in computing and electronics.

The breakthrough comes from a research team led by the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. In a study published in Science, the researchers presented compelling experimental evidence for altermagnetism, a distinct magnetic phase that combines important characteristics of the two traditionally recognized types.

"In the past few years, scientists have observed phenomena that don't fit neatly into the ferromagnetism-antiferromagnetism dichotomy," explained lead author Daniel Jost, associate scientist at SLAC and Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences. "Researchers have been compiling evidence of a third type of magnetism that bridges the qualities of these two classes. We believe our results provide robust experimental confirmation that this third phase -- altermagnetism -- is real."

The team focused on manganese telluride (MnTe), a material that had long been classified as an antiferromagnet. Building on earlier research, the scientists identified direct evidence of chirality, a distinctive asymmetry in the material's magnetic structure. This property resembles the way a spiral staircase or screw twists in a particular direction and provides a crucial signature of altermagnetism.

Beyond its importance for fundamental physics, the finding could help researchers develop magnetic materials with properties suited to future technologies, including advanced memory systems, quantum devices, and more energy-efficient data centers.

Understanding the Two Traditional Types of Magnetism

Magnetism is familiar from everyday experiences, whether it is a refrigerator magnet holding up a photograph or a compass aligning with Earth's magnetic field. But the physics behind these effects is far more complicated than it appears.

At the atomic level, magnetism is connected to a quantum property of electrons known as spin. Although spin is not literally an electron rotating like a tiny ball, it behaves in certain ways as though the electron has its own angular momentum. Scientists commonly describe the two possible spin orientations as "up" and "down."

When these spins become organized into particular patterns, a material can exhibit magnetic properties. However, that does not necessarily mean it will produce an externally detectable magnetic field.

In ferromagnetic materials, electron spins align in the same direction (up-up-up or down-down-down). Their combined effect produces the familiar magnetic field associated with ordinary magnets. People have used materials with this behavior for thousands of years.

A second category, identified in 1933, works differently. In antiferromagnets, neighboring electron spins point in opposite directions (up-down-up-down). Because the magnetic contributions oppose one another, they cancel out, leaving no overall magnetization.

A Third Type of Magnetism Challenges the Old Rules

For almost nine decades, these two categories provided the basic framework for understanding how magnetic order arises in materials. However, experimental observations in recent years began revealing behavior that neither category could fully explain.

Some materials displayed alternating electron spins and no overall magnetization, just like antiferromagnets. Yet they could also support useful spin currents, a property associated with ferromagnetic behavior. Spin currents allow information to be carried through the spin properties of electrons rather than relying entirely on their electrical charge.

The unusual combination suggested that scientists were dealing with something fundamentally different. In 2022, researchers introduced the term "altermagnets" for materials belonging to this proposed third magnetic class.

The key difference lies in the arrangement of atoms within the material. Altermagnets have alternating spin orientations (up-down-up-down), but the crystal structures surrounding the oppositely aligned spins are rotated relative to one another.

This rotation breaks a form of symmetry that exists in conventional antiferromagnets. Although the distinction is subtle, it can dramatically change how electrons behave, allowing altermagnets to combine properties once considered incompatible.

Scientists Find the Missing Evidence for Altermagnetism

Even as experimental support for altermagnetism accumulated, researchers still needed a decisive way to establish that it represented a genuinely distinct magnetic phase.

"By 2024, there were some factors that spoke strongly in favor of altermagnetism being real," Jost said, "but there was still a missing piece to the puzzle."

That missing evidence involved chirality, a property sometimes described as "handedness." An object is chiral when its mirror image cannot be perfectly aligned with the original. Human hands provide a simple example: Your left and right hands are mirror images, but a left hand cannot fit properly into a right-handed glove.

In an altermagnet, the unusual arrangement of atoms and electron spins can create this kind of handedness in the material's electronic and magnetic structure. Conventional antiferromagnets do not exhibit the same characteristic chiral signature.

Detecting that difference would provide a powerful way to distinguish a true altermagnet from a material that merely resembles one.

The researchers selected manganese telluride as their test material. For decades, scientists considered it an ordinary antiferromagnet, but more recent studies had raised the possibility that it belonged to the newly proposed category.

Powerful X-Rays Reveal a Hidden Magnetic Signature

To investigate the material's unusual properties, the team conducted experiments at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in France. The facility's ID32 beamline produces precisely controlled polarized X-rays, allowing scientists to examine subtle magnetic structures that are otherwise extremely difficult to detect.

The researchers used circularly polarized X-rays, which have electric fields that rotate in either a left-handed or right-handed direction as the light travels. By measuring how the material scattered these two forms of light, they could search for evidence of chirality.

"Chiral materials scatter left-handed polarized X-ray beams differently than they do right-handed beams," explained Jost. "Non-chiral materials would scatter each beam of light the same way."

The experiment revealed a clear difference in the way manganese telluride interacted with the two X-ray polarizations. This distinctive chiral response was precisely the kind of signal expected from altermagnetism and would not be present in a conventional antiferromagnet.

"This chiral signature gave us the solid experimental ground to say altermagnetism stands in a class of its own," Jost said.

The researchers first performed the experiment in 2024. They returned in early 2025 and repeated the measurements, successfully reproducing the results and strengthening the evidence for the new magnetic phase.

"This technique helped us confirm that manganese telluride was really exhibiting altermagnetic properties," said Rachel Nickel, postdoctoral scientist with ESRF, a co-author who helped design and conduct the experiment on the ID32 beamline. "Altermagnetism was only proposed a few years ago, and the rapid progress in confirming these models is incredible."

Why Altermagnetism Could Transform Future Computers

The discovery could have important consequences for spintronics, a growing field that seeks to use electron spin to develop more capable electronic devices.

Conventional electronics store and process information primarily by controlling the electrical charge of electrons. Spintronics adds another way to work with information by taking advantage of electron spin as well.

This extra capability could enable devices that operate faster, withstand interference more effectively, and consume substantially less electricity. Such improvements would be especially valuable in computer memory, large data centers, and other technologies that require enormous amounts of information processing.

However, the two traditional types of magnetism present different obstacles that have limited the development of spintronic systems.

"Ferromagnets are too easily influenced by magnetic fields," Jost explained. "If you have a permanent magnet in your pocket and walk by a spintronic device built with ferromagnets, you could start flipping the bits, scrambling the information stored there. Antiferromagnets fix that problem, but they are practically invisible -- so you can't easily read the data stored in them or use them to drive efficient spin currents."

Altermagnets offer a potentially valuable alternative. Like antiferromagnets, their opposing spins produce no overall magnetization, helping protect them against unwanted magnetic interference. At the same time, their unusual electronic structure allows them to generate spin-polarized currents that can be used to retrieve information.

"Altermagnets combine the best of both," Jost said. "They have zero net magnetization, so they're stable, but they still have the capability to generate spin-polarized currents needed to easily extract information. That gives you an additional degree of freedom to work with."

A New Frontier for Quantum Technology and Electronics

Confirming altermagnetism gives scientists a new class of materials to investigate and potentially engineer for technological applications. By combining magnetic stability with the ability to manipulate spin-based information, these materials could help overcome challenges that have held back conventional spintronic devices.

The next step will be learning how to control altermagnetic states using external influences such as light and electricity. Researchers hope that mastering this control will make it possible to design practical devices that take advantage of the unusual magnetic properties.

Although significant development is still needed before these materials can be widely used, the findings establish a stronger experimental foundation for future work on quantum technologies, computer memory, and more efficient data centers.
